joinZone.intro: This is a shared zone. Join it to co-manage its DNS records — you'll get your own TSIG key.

share.title: Share {{zone}}
share.intro: Everyone listed here manages this zone with equal rights. Each owner gets their own TSIG key; removing an owner deletes only their key, so the others keep working.
share.lastOwner: The last owner cannot be removed — delete the zone instead.
share.removeMessage: Remove {{owner}} from this zone? Their TSIG key is deleted and they lose access immediately. Other owners are unaffected.

keys.title: TSIG keys for {{zone}}
keys.intro: These are <1>TSIG</1> keys (Transaction SIGnature). Shared secrets that authenticate changes to this zone. Tools like <2>nsupdate</2>, cert-manager and external-dns use a key to update your records via <3>dynamic DNS updates</3> (<4>RFC 2136</4>) and zone transfers (AXFR). Anyone holding a key can modify the zone, so <5>keep it secret</5>.

records.title: DNS records for {{zone}}
records.intro: Add a record in the bottom row, or edit and delete existing ones inline. Changes take effect immediately.
records.searchPlaceholder: Search records by name, type, TTL, or value

noKey.snippets: This zone has no TSIG key yet — create one under the “Keys” tab first, then the snippets below will be filled in automatically.
noKey.dns01: This zone has no TSIG key yet — create one under the “Keys” tab first, then the DNS-01 example below will be filled in automatically.

dynamicDns.title: Dynamic DNS for {{zone}}
dynamicDns.intro: Keep a host's public IP current in this zone via <1>RFC 2136</1> — a one-shot <2>nsupdate</2> command, or <3>ddclient</3> for a self-running updater. Both use this zone's TSIG key.

oneShot.intro: Build a one-shot <1>nsupdate</1> command via <2>RFC 2136</2> (signed with this zone's TSIG key). Fill in the fields — the command below updates live. Run it once to create or update the record, and verify with <3>dig</3>.
oneShot.name: Name
oneShot.autoBody: To keep a record updated (e.g. a host whose public IP changes), save this command as a small script and run it on a schedule — for example with a <1>systemd timer</1> or a cron job. For a ready-made updater that also detects your current public IP, use the <2>ddclient</2> section below.

ddclient.intro: A self-running updater (<1>apt install ddclient</1>) that discovers this host's public address and keeps the record current. It uses the TSIG key file below via its <2>nsupdate</2> protocol. Use ddclient ≥ 3.10, which updates IPv4 and IPv6 independently (<3>usev4</3>/<4>usev6</4>) so a missing address never clears the other family. Adjust the interface (<5>eth0</5>) to yours.

recordName.label: Hostname to keep updated
recordName.description: The DNS name that should point at this machine's public IP, written relative to the zone (e.g. <1>my-host</1>). Use <2>@</2> to update the zone itself (its apex/root).
recordName.descriptionWithPreview: The DNS name that should point at this machine's public IP, written relative to the zone (e.g. <1>my-host</1> → <3>{{fqdn}}</3>). Use <2>@</2> to update the zone itself (its apex/root).

kubernetes.title: Dynamic DNS (Kubernetes) for {{zone}}
kubernetes.intro: Manage this zone's records from Kubernetes — either with <1>external-dns</1> in a cluster you already have, or by setting up a whole k3s cluster (DNS + HTTPS included) with the <2>k3s-dhbw-cloud-role</2> Ansible role. Both use this zone's TSIG key.
kubernetes.externalDnsIntro: Install <1>external-dns</1> into a cluster you already run, so this zone's records follow your Kubernetes resources (Services / Ingresses). It signs its updates with this zone's TSIG key.
kubernetes.step1: 1. Add the external-dns Helm repository (only once):
kubernetes.step2: 2. Save these values as <1>external-dns-values.yaml</1> — they carry this zone's TSIG key, so keep the file private:
kubernetes.ansibleIntro: Turn one or more fresh Linux hosts into a <1>k3s</1> cluster with the <2>k3s-dhbw-cloud-role</2> Ansible role. It installs external-dns and cert-manager for you, so every Ingress under this zone automatically gets a DNS record and a wildcard HTTPS certificate. Add the block below to your inventory — it is everything the role needs to know about this zone. Keep that file private: the TSIG key grants write access to the zone.

tls.title: TLS certificates for {{zone}}
tls.intro: Get certificates from the DHBW ACME server with <1>certbot</1>, <2>acme.sh</2>, or <3>cert-manager</3> (Kubernetes). All use DNS-01 (RFC 2136) with this zone's TSIG key and can issue <4>wildcard certificates</4>. The snippets below are pre-filled for this zone.
tls.certbotIntro: DNS-01 via the <1>certbot-dns-rfc2136</1> plugin. Issues wildcards too. First write the credentials file, then run certbot:
tls.acmeShIntro: DNS-01 via <1>nsupdate</1> (RFC 2136). First write the TSIG key file, then run acme.sh:
tls.namespaceDescription: Where the Certificate + TLS Secret go (your workload's namespace; i.e., where your ingresses live).
tls.dns01Intro: <1>DNS-01 (recommended)</1> — a <2>ClusterIssuer with the RFC 2136 solver</2> + this zone's TSIG key. No public HTTP access needed; can issue wildcards.
tls.http01Intro: <1>HTTP-01 (alternative)</1> — no TSIG, but the host must be reachable on :80 via an Ingress from inside the DHBW network. No wildcards.

policy.title: DNS Administration
policy.introEditable: Manage who may create which zones. Policy changes apply to new zones. Existing zones stay as they are, so plan any follow-up updates.
policy.introReadOnly: Read-only view of the DNS access rules that are currently active.
policy.searchPlaceholder: Search by zone pattern, user filter, or description...
policy.noRulesHint: Create the first rule to grant users access to DNS zones.
policy.subdomainsTooltip: Whether users may create subdomains (delegated subzones) under a matched zone
policy.sharingTooltip: Whether a matched zone may be shared with additional owners
policy.orphanWarning: Every zone that is covered <1>only</1> by this rule will become orphaned. Owners keep their DNS records, but can no longer manage those zones until a rule reproducing the same names and owners exists again — recreating it must match <2>exactly</2> (a single typo in the user filter is enough to leave the zones orphaned).

ruleForm.invalidFields: Please ensure Zone Pattern, Zone SOA, and User Filter are all valid.

ruleForm.soaDescription: The authoritative zone for this nameserver (e.g., users.example.com)
ruleForm.soaOutOfScope: Your delegations cover {{zones}} — the Zone SOA must be at or below one of these zones.
ruleForm.userFilterDescription: Comma-separated list. *@example.com = all users at that domain; alice@example.com = one specific user. Access is granted if any entry matches.
ruleForm.allowSubdomainsDescription: Owners of a matched zone may also create and manage delegated subzones under it (e.g. sub.example.com under example.com).
ruleForm.allowSharingDescription: Owners may share a matched zone with additional users, and policy-entitled users can join it as co-owners (equal rights). Off = single-owner (the old behaviour).
